results.name: Barn Owl (Tyto alba)
results.description:
Specimen: Barn Owl (Tyto alba)

The barn owl is the most widely distributed species of owl in the world and one of the most widespread of all species of birds, being found almost everywhere except for the polar and desert regions, Asia north of the Himalayas, most of Indonesia, and some Pacific Islands.

We'd love to hear from you if you download or print our models, particularly if you incorporate them into educational or outreach activities.

Contact us at: wattinstitution@inverclyde.gov.uk

results.name: Realistic Barn Owl 3D Model
results.description:
An elegant barn owl with a pale heart-shaped facial disc, soft cream and golden-buff speckled plumage, dark round eyes, and a small hooked beak. Shown in a neutral perched standing pose with wings folded, feathered legs and sharp curved talons clearly visible. This model was generated using AI-assisted 3D modeling as part of an ongoing wildlife asset pipeline, giving it clean, game-ready geometry. Suited for nature scenes, wildlife documentaries, rigging and animation, or realistic bird asset libraries. Realistic layered feather sculpting and detailed anatomy throughout.

results.name: Owl Wing in Ghost Town, Bodie California
results.description: Looking into a dirty window in the ghost town of Bodie California is a abandoned room with a large wing of a barn owl that meet a bad fate by being trapped and paniced.  Dead birds are one of the gristly, filthy, diseased, and disturbing things that one finds in ghost towns.  The scene evokes images of a nightmare for the owl and a place that you would not want to be in when it was happening.

results.name: Holycross Abbey (TN047-030001-) Owl
results.description: Holycross Abbey on the west bank of the River Suir, Co. Tipperary. A Cistercian abbey founded in 1180 possibly on the site of a Benedictine abbey by Donal O’Brien, King of Limerick in 1169. The late 12th-century ‘pilgrimage church’ of Holycross was rebuilt c. 1431.  Owl (barn owl/scréachóg reilige/graveyard screecher) with outstretched wings carved in relief on the south face of the northern pier of the crossing tower of Holycross Abbey. In medieval times the owl was a bird of bad news or bad luck. The owl as a nightime bird could represent the unbeliever who lived in the dark & was not enlightened by the teachings of Christianity. The bird is also associated in the Bible with misery, loneliness, ruin, destruction, mourning & grief. In Jeremiah 50:39 a person who is separated from God is like an owl who lives in rocky ravines and thrives in isolation. “I went mourning without the sun: I stood up, and I cried in the congregation. I am a brother to dragons and a companion to owls” (Job 30:28-29).
